claim: LRP1 is a multifunctional cell surface receptor with diverse physiological roles, ranging from cellular uptake of lipoproteins and other cargo by endocytosis to sensor of the extracellular environment and integrator of a wide range of signaling mechanisms.
source: Low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 1 (LRP1) is a multifunctional cell surface receptor with diverse physiological roles, ranging from cellular uptake of lipoproteins and other cargo by endocytosis to sensor of the extracellular environment and integrator of a wide range of signaling mechanisms.
evidence: This is a general characterization statement about LRP1 that draws from established scientific knowledge about this receptor's functions.

claim: As a chylomicron remnant receptor, LRP1 controls systemic lipid metabolism in concert with the LDL receptor in the liver.
source: As a chylomicron remnant receptor, LRP1 controls systemic lipid metabolism in concert with the LDL receptor in the liver, whereas in smooth muscle cells (SMC) LRP1 functions as a co-receptor for TGFβ and PDGFRβ in reverse cholesterol transport and the maintenance of vascular wall integrity.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about LRP1's role in lipid metabolism.

claim: In smooth muscle cells (SMC) LRP1 functions as a co-receptor for TGFβ and PDGFRβ in reverse cholesterol transport and the maintenance of vascular wall integrity.
source: As a chylomicron remnant receptor, LRP1 controls systemic lipid metabolism in concert with the LDL receptor in the liver, whereas in smooth muscle cells (SMC) LRP1 functions as a co-receptor for TGFβ and PDGFRβ in reverse cholesterol transport and the maintenance of vascular wall integrity.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about LRP1's role in smooth muscle cells.

claim: Tyrosine phosphorylation of an NPxY motif in LRP1's intracellular domain initiates a signaling cascade along an LRP1/SHC1/PI3K/AKT/PPARγ/LXR axis.
source: Here we used a knockin mouse model to uncover a novel atheroprotective role for LRP1 in macrophages where tyrosine phosphorylation of an NPxY motif in its intracellular domain initiates a signaling cascade along an LRP1/SHC1/PI3K/AKT/PPARγ/LXR axis to regulate and integrate cellular cholesterol homeostasis through the expression of the major cholesterol exporter ABCA1 with apoptotic cell removal and inflammatory responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the knockin mouse model described in the manuscript.

claim: The LRP1/SHC1/PI3K/AKT/PPARγ/LXR axis regulates cellular cholesterol homeostasis through the expression of ABCA1.
source: Here we used a knockin mouse model to uncover a novel atheroprotective role for LRP1 in macrophages where tyrosine phosphorylation of an NPxY motif in its intracellular domain initiates a signaling cascade along an LRP1/SHC1/PI3K/AKT/PPARγ/LXR axis to regulate and integrate cellular cholesterol homeostasis through the expression of the major cholesterol exporter ABCA1 with apoptotic cell removal and inflammatory responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the knockin mouse model.

claim: Atherosclerosis is a chronic condition characterized by impairments in three major processes: systemic and cellular cholesterol homeostasis, inflammation, and apoptosis/efferocytosis.
source: Atherosclerosis is a chronic condition characterized by impairments in three major processes: systemic and cellular cholesterol homeostasis, inflammation, and apoptosis/efferocytosis (Libby et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Libby et al., 2011.

claim: Essential roles for LRP1 have been reported for cholesterol homeostasis, inflammation, and apoptosis/efferocytosis.
source: Essential roles for the multifunctional transmembrane protein LDL receptor-related-protein 1 (LRP1) have been reported for each of these three processes (Boucher et al., 2003; Boucher et al., 2002; El Asmar et al., 2016; Mantuano et al., 2016; Subramanian et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2009a; Zurhove et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Together with LDLR, LRP1 regulates the clearance of circulating cholesterol-rich remnant proteins by hepatocytes.
source: Together with LDLR, LRP1 regulates the clearance of circulating cholesterol-rich remnant proteins by hepatocytes (Rohlmann et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rohlmann et al., 1998.

claim: LRP1 is a key regulator of intracellular cholesterol accumulation in macrophages and smooth muscle cells (SMCs).
source: LRP1 is also a key regulator of intracellular cholesterol accumulation in macrophages and smooth muscle cells (SMCs) (Boucher et al., 2003; Lillis et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2009a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In SMCs, LRP1 functions as a co-receptor with platelet-derived growth factor receptor (PDGFRβ), which in turn activates inflammatory and pro-thrombotic processes.
source: In SMCs, LRP1 functions as a co-receptor with platelet-derived growth factor receptor (PDGFRβ), which in turn activates inflammatory and pro-thrombotic processes (Boucher et al., 2002; Loukinova et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LRP1 has been implicated in limiting cellular inflammatory responses.
source: LRP1 itself has also been implicated in limiting cellular inflammatory responses (Mantuano et al., 2016; Zurhove et al., 2008), and the dual role of LRP1 in cholesterol homeostasis and inflammation (El Asmar et al., 2016; Woldt et al., 2011, 2012) was recently demonstrated in an adipocyte-specific LRP1-deficient mouse model (Konaniah et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The dual role of LRP1 in cholesterol homeostasis and inflammation was demonstrated in an adipocyte-specific LRP1-deficient mouse model.
source: LRP1 itself has also been implicated in limiting cellular inflammatory responses (Mantuano et al., 2016; Zurhove et al., 2008), and the dual role of LRP1 in cholesterol homeostasis and inflammation (El Asmar et al., 2016; Woldt et al., 2011, 2012) was recently demonstrated in an adipocyte-specific LRP1-deficient mouse model (Konaniah et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Konaniah et al., 2017.

claim: LRP1 is necessary for efficient efferocytosis in macrophages and dendritic cells.
source: Finally, LRP1 is necessary for efficient efferocytosis in macrophages and dendritic cells (Subramanian et al., 2014; Yancey et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LRP1 is ubiquitously expressed, but how it affects cellular signaling mechanisms can differ substantially in a cell-type dependent manner.
source: LRP1 is ubiquitously expressed, but how it affects cellular signaling mechanisms can differ substantially in a cell-type dependent manner.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about LRP1 expression patterns.

claim: In SMCs, LRP1 regulates ERK1/2 activation, which leads to increased cPLA2 phosphorylation and release of arachidonic acid.
source: In SMCs, LRP1 regulates ERK1/2 activation, which leads to increased cPLA2 phosphorylation and release of arachidonic acid (Graves et al., 1996; Lin et al., 1992), a suppressor of LXR-driven ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1) expression (DeBose-Boyd et al., 2001), thereby increasing SMC intracellular cholesterol accumulation (Zhou et al., 2009a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Arachidonic acid is a suppressor of LXR-driven ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1) expression.
source: In SMCs, LRP1 regulates ERK1/2 activation, which leads to increased cPLA2 phosphorylation and release of arachidonic acid (Graves et al., 1996; Lin et al., 1992), a suppressor of LXR-driven ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1) expression (DeBose-Boyd et al., 2001), thereby increasing SMC intracellular cholesterol accumulation (Zhou et al., 2009a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to DeBose-Boyd et al., 2001.

claim: ABCA1 mediates reverse cholesterol export.
source: ABCA1, however, mediates not just reverse cholesterol export, it also regulates cellular inflammatory responses (Ito et al., 2015; Tang et al., 2009; Zhu et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about ABCA1 function.

claim: ABCA1 regulates cellular inflammatory responses.
source: ABCA1, however, mediates not just reverse cholesterol export, it also regulates cellular inflammatory responses (Ito et al., 2015; Tang et al., 2009; Zhu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is an LRP1/LXR/ABCA1 axis that controls and integrates cellular cholesterol export and inflammatory responses.
source: This suggests the presence of an LRP1/LXR/ABCA1 axis that controls and integrates cellular cholesterol export and inflammatory responses.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the previous statements about LRP1, LXR, and ABCA1.

claim: One of the atheroprotective roles of LRP1 in the vascular wall is the regulation of the mitogenic pathway mediated by platelet derived growth factor (PDGF).
source: One of the atheroprotective roles of LRP1 in the vascular wall is the regulation of the well-established mitogenic pathway mediated by platelet derived growth factor (PDGF), which promotes atherosclerosis (Ross, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ross, 1993.

claim: PDGF promotes atherosclerosis.
source: One of the atheroprotective roles of LRP1 in the vascular wall is the regulation of the well-established mitogenic pathway mediated by platelet derived growth factor (PDGF), which promotes atherosclerosis (Ross, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ross, 1993.

claim: Stimulation of PDGFRβ with PDGF-BB induces tyrosine phosphorylation of LRP1 by Src-family tyrosine kinases at the distal cytoplasmic NPxY motif.
source: Mitogenic signaling is commonly associated with tyrosine phosphorylation, and stimulation of PDGFRβ with PDGF-BB induces tyrosine phosphorylation of LRP1 by Src-family tyrosine kinases at the distal cytoplasmic NPxY motif (Barnes et al., 2001; Boucher et al., 2002; Loukinova et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Phosphorylation of LRP1 can either promote or inhibit the association of the LRP1-ICD with several intracellular adaptor proteins, which in turn modulates down-stream signaling cascades.
source: This phosphorylation event can either promote or inhibit the association of the LRP1-ICD (intracellular domain) with several intracellular adaptor proteins, which in turn modulates down-stream signaling cascades (Gotthardt et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gotthardt et al., 2000.

claim: The physiological significance of LRP1 NPxY phosphorylation has remained unclear.
source: However, the physiological significance of LRP1 NPxY phosphorylation has remained unclear.
evidence: This statement acknowledges a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: A knock-in mouse model was developed in which the tyrosine in the distal NPxY motif was replaced with phenylalanine (Lrp1Y63F).
source: To investigate this role of LRP1 tyrosine phosphorylation in atherosclerosis, we developed a knock-in mouse model in which the tyrosine in the distal NPxY motif was replaced with phenylalanine (Lrp1Y63F), thereby disabling Lrp1 NPxY phosphorylation while leaving the interaction with phosphotyrosine-independent PTB-domain containing adaptor proteins intact (Gotthardt et al., 2000; Trommsdorff et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental model created for this study.

claim: The Lrp1Y63F mutation disables Lrp1 NPxY phosphorylation while leaving the interaction with phosphotyrosine-independent PTB-domain containing adaptor proteins intact.
source: To investigate this role of LRP1 tyrosine phosphorylation in atherosclerosis, we developed a knock-in mouse model in which the tyrosine in the distal NPxY motif was replaced with phenylalanine (Lrp1Y63F), thereby disabling Lrp1 NPxY phosphorylation while leaving the interaction with phosphotyrosine-independent PTB-domain containing adaptor proteins intact (Gotthardt et al., 2000; Trommsdorff et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental design and citations to previous studies.

claim: LRP1 NPxY phosphorylation induces a molecular switch of associated cytoplasmic adaptor proteins away from endocytosis-promoting DAB2 to the signal-transducer SHC1.
source: We found that LRP1 NPxY phosphorylation induces a molecular switch of associated cytoplasmic adaptor proteins away from endocytosis-promoting DAB2 to the well-known signal-transducer SHC1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: SHC1 is an evolutionarily conserved adaptor protein that mediates mitogenic signaling.
source: SHC1 is an evolutionarily conserved adaptor protein that mediates mitogenic signaling (Dieckmann et al., 2010; Pelicci et al., 1992; van der Geer, 2002; van der Geer and Pawson, 1995; van der Geer et al., 1995) and is required for LRP1-dependent signal transduction in SMC through activation of PI3K and phosphorylation of AKT (Gu et al., 2000; Radhakrishnan et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SHC1 is required for LRP1-dependent signal transduction in SMC through activation of PI3K and phosphorylation of AKT.
source: SHC1 is an evolutionarily conserved adaptor protein that mediates mitogenic signaling (Dieckmann et al., 2010; Pelicci et al., 1992; van der Geer, 2002; van der Geer and Pawson, 1995; van der Geer et al., 1995) and is required for LRP1-dependent signal transduction in SMC through activation of PI3K and phosphorylation of AKT (Gu et al., 2000; Radhakrishnan et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Lack of LRP1 tyrosine phosphorylation was inconsequential in SMCs.
source: Surprisingly, lack of LRP1 tyrosine phosphorylation was inconsequential in SMCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: In macrophages, SHC1 binding to phosphorylated LRP1 activated PI3K/AKT and PPARγ/LXR driven ABCA1 expression.
source: By contrast, in macrophages, SHC1 binding to phosphorylated LRP1 activated PI3K/AKT and PPARγ/LXR driven ABCA1 expression, a major cellular cholesterol exporter, and one of many mechanisms that is impaired in atherogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Disabling LRP1 tyrosine phosphorylation resulted in enhanced macrophage intracellular lipid accumulation and decreased clearance of apoptotic cells.
source: Consequently, disabling LRP1 tyrosine phosphorylation resulted in enhanced macrophage intracellular lipid accumulation and decreased clearance of apoptotic cells, thus resulting in accelerated atherosclerosis independent of plasma cholesterol levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Disabling LRP1 tyrosine phosphorylation resulted in accelerated atherosclerosis independent of plasma cholesterol levels.
source: Consequently, disabling LRP1 tyrosine phosphorylation resulted in enhanced macrophage intracellular lipid accumulation and decreased clearance of apoptotic cells, thus resulting in accelerated atherosclerosis independent of plasma cholesterol levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Western blot analysis of liver and aortic extracts from Lrp1Y63F mice revealed no effect of the Y63F mutation on Lrp1 expression in the liver or the aorta.
source: Western blot analysis of liver and aortic extracts from Lrp1Y63F mice revealed no effect of the Y63F mutation on Lrp1 expression in the liver or the aorta (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Pull-down experiments in SMC stimulated with PDGF-BB confirmed decreased phosphorylation of the Lrp1 cytoplasmic domain in Lrp1Y63F SMC when compared with wild type SMC.
source: Pull-down experiments in SMC stimulated with PDGF-BB confirmed decreased phosphorylation of the Lrp1 cytoplasmic domain in Lrp1Y63F SMC when compared with wild type SMC (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by pull-down experiment data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: After stimulation of wild type SMC with PDGF-BB, Shc1 was bound to Lrp1, but Dab2 was not.
source: After stimulation of wild type SMC with PDGF-BB, which induces phosphorylation of the distal NPxY motif in the Lrp1 cytoplasmic domain, Shc1 was bound to Lrp1, but Dab2 was not.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: In Lrp1Y63F SMC, Shc1 was no longer able to bind to Lrp1, while Dab2 could be co-immunoprecipitated with Lrp1.
source: In Lrp1Y63F SMC, in which phosphorylation of the distal NPxY motif is prevented, Shc1 was no longer able to bind to Lrp1, while Dab2 could now be co-immunoprecipitated with Lrp1 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Binding of Shc1 to Lrp1 is regulated by tyrosine phosphorylation of the distal NPxY motif of Lrp1.
source: Thus, binding of Shc1 to Lrp1 is regulated by tyrosine phosphorylation of the distal NPxY motif of Lrp1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation data showing differential binding patterns.

claim: Body weight, plasma cholesterol and triglyceride concentrations of Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice on chow diet were essentially identical to age and sex-matched Ldlr−/− controls.
source: Body weight, plasma cholesterol and triglyceride concentrations of Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice on chow diet were essentially identical to age and sex-matched Ldlr−/− controls (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: After 16 weeks on HCHF diet, Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice had significantly increased body weight compared to Ldlr−/− mice.
source: However, after 16 weeks on HCHF diet, Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice had significantly increased body weight, plasma cholesterol (2035 ± 99.53 mg/dl vs. 1672 ± 45.98 mg/dl, p<0.01) and triglyceride levels (257.4 ± 26.2 mg/dl vs. 161.8 ± 13.55 mg/dl, p<0.01) compared to Ldlr−/− mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: After 16 weeks on HCHF diet, Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice had significantly increased plasma cholesterol (2035 ± 99.53 mg/dl vs. 1672 ± 45.98 mg/dl, p<0.01) compared to Ldlr−/− mice.
source: However, after 16 weeks on HCHF diet, Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice had significantly increased body weight, plasma cholesterol (2035 ± 99.53 mg/dl vs. 1672 ± 45.98 mg/dl, p<0.01) and triglyceride levels (257.4 ± 26.2 mg/dl vs. 161.8 ± 13.55 mg/dl, p<0.01) compared to Ldlr−/− mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: After 16 weeks on HCHF diet, Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice had significantly increased triglyceride levels (257.4 ± 26.2 mg/dl vs. 161.8 ± 13.55 mg/dl, p<0.01) compared to Ldlr−/− mice.
source: However, after 16 weeks on HCHF diet, Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice had significantly increased body weight, plasma cholesterol (2035 ± 99.53 mg/dl vs. 1672 ± 45.98 mg/dl, p<0.01) and triglyceride levels (257.4 ± 26.2 mg/dl vs. 161.8 ± 13.55 mg/dl, p<0.01) compared to Ldlr−/− mice (Figure 2A).

claim: Western blot analysis revealed increased ApoB48 and ApoE in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice after HCHF diet feeding.
source: Western blot analysis revealed increased ApoB48 and ApoE in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice, whereas ApoB100 and ApoAI were decreased compared to Ldlr−/− mice after HCHF diet feeding (Figure 2B).

claim: ApoB100 and ApoAI were decreased in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice compared to Ldlr−/− mice after HCHF diet feeding.
source: Western blot analysis revealed increased ApoB48 and ApoE in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice, whereas ApoB100 and ApoAI were decreased compared to Ldlr−/− mice after HCHF diet feeding (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: FPLC lipoprotein analysis demonstrated that elevated plasma cholesterol levels in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice fed with HCHF diet were attributed to increased VLDL-cholesterol with slightly reduced LDL- and HDL-cholesterol contents.
source: FPLC lipoprotein analysis demonstrated that elevated plasma cholesterol levels in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice fed with HCHF diet were attributed to increased VLDL-cholesterol with slightly reduced LDL- and HDL-cholesterol contents (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FPLC data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: VLDL-triglyceride levels were increased in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice.
source: VLDL-triglyceride levels were also increased in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FPLC data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Size-fractionated ApoB100 and ApoAI were significantly decreased, but ApoE was increased in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice.
source: Consistent with the results of total plasma apolipoprotein analysis, size-fractionated ApoB100 and ApoAI were significantly decreased, but ApoE was increased in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ApoB48 remnant particles were shifted towards a larger size in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice compared to Ldlr−/− mice on HCHF diet.
source: Interestingly, ApoB48 remnant particles were shifted towards a larger size in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice compared to Ldlr−/− mice on HCHF diet, possibly suggesting impaired clearance through SR-B1 (Rigotti et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by data and includes speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The Lrp1Y63F mutation promotes the accumulation of ApoB48 remnants, as also seen in the hepatic Lrp1 knockout.
source: We conclude that the Lrp1Y63F mutation not only promotes the accumulation of ApoB48 remnants, as also seen in the hepatic Lrp1 knockout (Rohlmann et al., 1998; Rohlmann et al., 1996), but also causes decreases in HDL and ApoA1, which could independently increase atherosclerosis reminiscent of the increased risk of premature atherosclerosis in individuals with Tangier's disease (Tall and Wang, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The Lrp1Y63F mutation causes decreases in HDL and ApoA1, which could independently increase atherosclerosis.
source: We conclude that the Lrp1Y63F mutation not only promotes the accumulation of ApoB48 remnants, as also seen in the hepatic Lrp1 knockout (Rohlmann et al., 1998; Rohlmann et al., 1996), but also causes decreases in HDL and ApoA1, which could independently increase atherosclerosis reminiscent of the increased risk of premature atherosclerosis in individuals with Tangier's disease (Tall and Wang, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by data and includes speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Compared to Ldlr−/− mice, Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice showed a 1.7-fold increase of atherosclerotic lesion area throughout the entire aorta.
source: Compared to Ldlr−/− mice, Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice showed a 1.7-fold and 2.7-fold increase of atherosclerotic lesion area throughout the entire aorta and in the aortic root, respectively (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Compared to Ldlr−/− mice, Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice showed a 2.7-fold increase of atherosclerotic lesion area in the aortic root.
source: Compared to Ldlr−/− mice, Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice showed a 1.7-fold and 2.7-fold increase of atherosclerotic lesion area throughout the entire aorta and in the aortic root, respectively (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Smooth muscle Lrp1 deficiency leads to increased SMC proliferation and migration and retention of cholesterol, leading to profound aortic atherosclerosis.
source: Our previous studies demonstrated that smooth muscle Lrp1 deficiency leads to increased SMC proliferation and migration and retention of cholesterol, leading to profound aortic atherosclerosis.
evidence: This claim refers to previous studies by the authors.

claim: The SMC-targeted Lrp1 knockout mouse model (smLrp1−/−) displays prominent aortic wall thickening and increased numbers of SMC even under normolipidemic conditions.
source: Unlike the SMC-targeted Lrp1 knockout mouse model (smLrp1−/−), which displays prominent aortic wall thickening and increased numbers of SMC even under normolipidemic conditions, morphometric analysis of the thoracic aorta from Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− and Ldlr−/− mice revealed no difference in aortic wall thickness or numbers of SMC (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Morphometric analysis of the thoracic aorta from Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− and Ldlr−/− mice revealed no difference in aortic wall thickness or numbers of SMC.
source: Unlike the SMC-targeted Lrp1 knockout mouse model (smLrp1−/−), which displays prominent aortic wall thickening and increased numbers of SMC even under normolipidemic conditions, morphometric analysis of the thoracic aorta from Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− and Ldlr−/− mice revealed no difference in aortic wall thickness or numbers of SMC (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Analysis of whole aorta homogenate from the Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− and Ldlr−/− mice showed no significant differences in the activation of known PDGF down-stream signal effectors.
source: Furthermore, analysis of whole aorta homogenate (Figure 4B) and explanted primary aortic SMC (Figure 4C) from the Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− and Ldlr−/− mice showed no significant differences in the activation of known PDGF down-stream signal effectors.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: No difference in migration or proliferation was observed between wild type and Lrp1Y63F SMC.
source: Finally, to test the functional properties of the explanted SMC, we used Transwell Migration and BrdU Proliferation assays to compare their migratory and proliferative response to PDGF-BB. No difference in migration or proliferation was observed between wild type and Lrp1Y63F SMC (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The Lrp1Y63F mutation does not increase atherosclerosis propensity through a change of SMC phenotype.
source: We therefore concluded that the Lrp1Y63F mutation does not increase atherosclerosis propensity through a change of SMC phenotype.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing no changes in SMC function.

claim: Semi-quantitative, cross-sectional analysis of the composition of atherosclerotic lesions in the aortic sinus revealed a 57% increase in Mac-3–positive macrophages in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice.
source: Semi-quantitative, cross-sectional analysis of the composition of atherosclerotic lesions in the aortic sinus revealed a 57% increase in Mac-3–positive macrophages, but a comparable amount of α-actin–positive cells (corresponding to SMC) in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice, consistent with a pronounced infiltration of macrophages into the atherosclerotic plaque (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There was a comparable amount of α-actin–positive cells (corresponding to SMC) in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice.
source: Semi-quantitative, cross-sectional analysis of the composition of atherosclerotic lesions in the aortic sinus revealed a 57% increase in Mac-3–positive macrophages, but a comparable amount of α-actin–positive cells (corresponding to SMC) in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice, consistent with a pronounced infiltration of macrophages into the atherosclerotic plaque (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Semi-quantitative analysis of H&E staining showed a 40% increase in necrotic core area in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice.
source: Further semi-quantitative analysis of H&E staining showed a 40% increase in necrotic core area in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The increase in apoptosis was confirmed by TUNEL staining of atherosclerotic plaques in vivo.
source: The increase in apoptosis was confirmed by TUNEL staining of atherosclerotic plaques in vivo (Figure 5C) and oxLDL loaded peritoneal macrophages in vitro (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: Deficiency in MER proto-oncogene tyrosine kinase (MerTK) is associated with increased macrophage apoptosis and decreased efferocytosis, leading to increased necrotic cores in Apoe−/− mice.
source: Deficiency in MER proto-oncogene tyrosine kinase (MerTK) is associated with increased macrophage apoptosis and decreased efferocytosis, leading to increased necrotic cores in Apoe−/− mice (Li et al., 2006; Scott et al., 2001; Thorp et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Peritoneal macrophages from Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice showed a significant decrease in MerTK expression both at baseline and in response to treatment with oxLDL.
source: We isolated peritoneal macrophages from Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− and control mice and found a significant decrease in MerTK expression both at baseline and in response to treatment with oxLDL (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Increased necrotic core size and apoptosis in the Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice may be attributed at least in part to MerTK dysfunction associated with the macrophage Lrp1 mutation.
source: Therefore, increased necrotic core size and apoptosis in the Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice may be attributed at least in part to MerTK dysfunction associated with the macrophage Lrp1 mutation, in addition to other efferocytosis-related functions that are controlled by LRP1 (Subramanian et al., 2014; Yancey et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The striking increase in atherosclerosis in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice is due to macrophages and not SMCs.
source: Based on these results, we suspected that the striking increase in atherosclerosis in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice is due to macrophages and not SMCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing macrophage dysfunction but no SMC changes.

claim: After 16 weeks of HCHF diet all irradiated mouse groups that underwent bone marrow transplant exhibited high plasma cholesterol levels.
source: After 16 weeks of HCHF diet all irradiated mouse groups that underwent bone marrow transplant exhibited high plasma cholesterol levels (Figure 6A).

claim: There was no difference in plasma lipid and apolipoprotein levels between Ldlr−/− → Ldlr−/− and Lrp1Y63F; Ldlr−/− → Ldlr−/− mice.

claim: The Lrp1Y63F mutation in macrophages is not responsible for the changes in the lipid profile.
source: By comparing Figure 6C to Figure 2C, we demonstrated that bone marrow transplantation eliminated the difference in peripheral lipid profiles, thereby demonstrating that the Lrp1Y63F mutation in macrophages is not responsible for the changes in the lipid profile.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the bone marrow transplantation data.

claim: The correction of HDL and ApoA1 levels in the bone marrow transplant model suggested a role for Y63 phosphorylation in the liver.
source: Furthermore, the correction of HDL and ApoA1 levels in the bone marrow transplant model suggested a role for Y63 phosphorylation in the liver.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the bone marrow transplantation data.

claim: Increased catabolism of ApoA1 is a hallmark of the functional impairment of ABCA1 in Tangier's disease.
source: Increased catabolism of ApoA1 is a hallmark of the functional impairment of ABCA1 in Tangier's disease (Tall and Wang, 2000) and in liver Abca1 deficient mice (Timmins et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: After a 16 week HCHF diet challenge, Western blot analysis showed decreased expression of Abca1 in the liver from Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice.
source: After a 16 week HCHF diet challenge, Western blot analysis showed decreased expression of Abca1 in the liver from Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice (Figure 7A), but no change in Abca1 expression in the liver of Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− → Ldlr−/− mice (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: There was no change in Abca1 expression in the liver of Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− → Ldlr−/− mice.
source: After a 16 week HCHF diet challenge, Western blot analysis showed decreased expression of Abca1 in the liver from Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice (Figure 7A), but no change in Abca1 expression in the liver of Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− → Ldlr−/− mice (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The significant decrease in hepatic Abca1 likely accounts for the decreased plasma ApoA1 in the Lrp1Y63F mouse.
source: Therefore, as in Tangier's disease, the significant decrease in hepatic Abca1 likely accounts for the decreased plasma ApoA1 in the Lrp1Y63F mouse.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing decreased hepatic Abca1 and decreased plasma ApoA1.

claim: Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− → Ldlr−/− still developed more atherosclerotic lesions when compared to Ldlr−/− → Ldlr−/− controls on HCHF diet.
source: However, even though hepatic Abca1 expression (and therefore plasma ApoA1 levels) is normalized in the bone marrow transplantation model, Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− → Ldlr−/− still developed more atherosclerotic lesions when compared to Ldlr−/− → Ldlr−/− controls on HCHF diet (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The relatively modest change in lipoprotein profiles is insufficient to explain the striking increase in atherosclerosis generated by the Lrp1Y63F mutation.
source: These results indicate that the relatively modest change in lipoprotein profiles (increased chylomicrons and decreased HDL) is insufficient to explain the striking increase in atherosclerosis generated by the Lrp1Y63F mutation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the bone marrow transplantation data.

claim: A cell autonomous effect of Lrp1 tyrosine phosphorylation in macrophages is primarily responsible for increased atherosclerosis.
source: Instead, a cell autonomous effect of Lrp1 tyrosine phosphorylation in macrophages is primarily responsible for increased atherosclerosis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the bone marrow transplantation data.

claim: Intracellular lipid accumulation was significantly higher in cultured Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− macrophages compared to control cells as shown by Oil-Red O staining.
source: Intracellular lipid accumulation was significantly higher in cultured Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− macrophages compared to control cells as shown by Oil-Red O staining (Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Oil-Red O staining data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Macrophages from Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice had significantly reduced cholesterol efflux capacity to ApoAI, but not to HDL.
source: Compared to Ldlr−/−, macrophages from Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice had significantly reduced cholesterol efflux capacity to ApoAI, but not to HDL (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cholesterol efflux data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: In response to oxLDL, Cd36 was increased in Ldlr−/− and Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− macrophages.
source: In response to oxLDL, Cd36 was increased in Ldlr−/− and Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data.

claim: There was decreased expression of the reverse cholesterol transporter Abca1 both at baseline and in response to oxLDL in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− macrophages.
source: However, there was decreased expression of the reverse cholesterol transporter Abca1 both at baseline and in response to oxLDL in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− macrophages, consistent with the cholesterol efflux data.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: No difference in the expression levels of Abcg1 and Srb1 were observed in the two genotypes after oxLDL stimulation.
source: No difference in the expression levels of Abcg1 and Srb1 were observed in the two genotypes after oxLDL stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Analysis of surface and total expression of Abca1 and Lrp1 in oxLDL-stimulated macrophages revealed no difference in the ratio of surface/total Abca1 or Lrp1 between Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− and Ldlr−/− macrophages.
source: Analysis of surface and total expression of Abca1 and Lrp1 in oxLDL-stimulated macrophages revealed no difference in the ratio of surface/total Abca1 or Lrp1 between Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− and Ldlr−/− macrophages (Figure 9D), suggesting that translocation of Abca1 and Lrp1 to the cell membrane is functioning normally.
evidence: This claim is supported by surface biotinylation data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Cross-sectional analysis of the aortic root confirmed greatly decreased expression of Abca1 in atherosclerotic plaques from HCHF diet fed Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice in vivo.
source: Finally, cross-sectional analysis of the aortic root confirmed greatly decreased expression of Abca1 in atherosclerotic plaques from HCHF diet fed Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice in vivo (Figure 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 10.

claim: Macrophage cholesterol efflux through Abca1 is selectively impaired by the Lrp1Y63F mutation.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that macrophage cholesterol efflux through Abca1 is selectively impaired by the Lrp1Y63F mutation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing decreased Abca1 expression and reduced cholesterol efflux to ApoAI.

claim: A major regulator of ABCA1 expression is LXR: both LXRα and LXRβ respond to oxidized sterols and regulate cholesterol transport.
source: A major regulator of ABCA1 expression is LXR: both LXRα and LXRβ respond to oxidized sterols and regulate cholesterol transport (Janowski et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Janowski et al., 1996.

claim: In macrophages, activation of PPARγ induces LXRα transcriptional activation, thereby increasing ABCA1 expression.
source: In macrophages, activation of PPARγ induces LXRα transcriptional activation, thereby increasing ABCA1 expression (Chawla et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chawla et al., 2001.

claim: LRP1 indirectly regulates LXR-mediated ABCA1 expression independent of LXR gene transcription in SMC.
source: We have previously shown in SMC that LRP1 indirectly regulates LXR-mediated ABCA1 expression independent of LXR gene transcription (Zhou et al., 2009a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The LRP1 cytoplasmic domain can regulate gene expression by directly interacting with PPARγ.
source: An additional precedent is provided by a recent study demonstrating that the LRP1 cytoplasmic domain itself can regulate gene expression by directly interacting with PPARγ (Mao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mao et al., 2017.

claim: The Lrp1Y63F mutation diminished oxLDL-induced Abca1 gene transcription, but not Abca7 gene transcription.
source: The Lrp1Y63F mutation diminished oxLDL-induced Abca1 gene transcription, but not Abca7 gene transcription, which by contrast is increased in macrophages lacking LRP1 completely (Yancey et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 11A.

claim: The Lrp1Y63F mutation had no effect on Nr1h3 (a.k.a. Lxrα), Nr2h2 (a.k.a. Lxrβ), or Pparg gene expression in macrophages in the presence or absence of oxLDL.
source: Furthermore, the Lrp1Y63F mutation had no effect on Nr1h3 (a.k.a. Lxrα), Nr2h2 (a.k.a. Lxrβ), or Pparg gene expression in macrophages in the presence or absence of oxLDL (Figure 11A), and there was no change in LXRα or PPARγ protein expression (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 11A.

claim: PPARγ activity was necessary for Abca1 expression in both Ldlr−/− and Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− macrophages.
source: Using the PPARγ inhibitor T0070907, we confirmed that PPARγ activity was necessary for Abca1 expression in both Ldlr−/− and Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− macrophages (Figure 11B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11B.

claim: Neither LXR or PPARγ agonists, over a range of doses, were able to fully correct the blunted Abca1 levels in the Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice.
source: Neither LXR or PPARγ agonists, over a range of doses, were able to fully correct the blunted Abca1 levels in the Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice (Figure 11C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11C-E.

claim: The entire PPARγ/LXR/ABCA1 axis is severely impaired by the Lrp1Y63F mutation in macrophages.
source: Together these data demonstrate that the entire PPARγ/LXR/ABCA1 axis is severely impaired by the Lrp1Y63F mutation in macrophages and suggest that a membrane proximal event that is dependent on Lrp1 tyrosine phosphorylation is required to activate Abca1 transcription through PPARγ and LXR.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing impaired response to PPARγ and LXR agonists.

claim: A membrane proximal event that is dependent on Lrp1 tyrosine phosphorylation is required to activate Abca1 transcription through PPARγ and LXR.
source: Together these data demonstrate that the entire PPARγ/LXR/ABCA1 axis is severely impaired by the Lrp1Y63F mutation in macrophages and suggest that a membrane proximal event that is dependent on Lrp1 tyrosine phosphorylation is required to activate Abca1 transcription through PPARγ and LXR.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing impaired response to PPARγ and LXR agonists.

claim: LRP1 regulates mitogenic signaling, leading to ERK and AKT phosphorylation in SMCs.
source: We have previously shown in SMCs that LRP1 regulates mitogenic signaling, leading to ERK and AKT phosphorylation (Boucher et al., 2003; Zhou et al., 2009b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: PI3K/AKT activation can modulate the PPARγ/LXR/ABCA1 axis.
source: Demers et al. showed that PI3K/AKT activation can modulate the PPARγ/LXR/ABCA1 axis (Demers et al., 2009), thereby raising the possibility that PI3K activation might be dependent upon LRP1.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Demers et al., 2009.

claim: Phospho-Akt levels were significantly decreased in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− macrophages, both at baseline and in response to oxLDL.
source: Phospho-Akt levels were significantly decreased in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− macrophages, both at baseline and in response to oxLDL (Figure 12A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 12A.

claim: Inhibition of the PI3K/Akt pathway with LY294002 or an Akt inhibitor in Ldlr−/− macrophages significantly attenuated Abca1 induction in response to oxLDL.
source: Moreover, inhibition of the PI3K/Akt pathway with LY294002, a PI3K inhibitor, or an Akt inhibitor, in Ldlr−/− macrophages significantly attenuated Abca1 induction in response to oxLDL, such that Abca1 expression levels were comparable to those found in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− macrophages (Figure 12B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 12B.

claim: Inhibition of PI3K/Akt results in incomplete induction of Abca1 by both PPARγ and LXR agonists.
source: Inhibition of PI3K/Akt results in incomplete induction of Abca1 by both PPARγ and LXR agonists, similar to what is observed in macrophages carrying the Lrp1Y63F mutation (Figure 12C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 12C and D.

claim: There is an endogenous mechanism that is dependent upon LRP1 tyrosine phosphorylation to activate PI3K/Akt and subsequently PPARγ/LXR-induced Abca1 expression.
source: This suggested the existence of an endogenous mechanism that is dependent upon LRP1 tyrosine phosphorylation to activate PI3K/Akt and subsequently PPARγ/LXR-induced Abca1 expression.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing the effects of PI3K/Akt inhibition.

claim: The interaction between phosphorylated Lrp1 and Shc1 occurs in macrophages.
source: Using co-immunoprecipitation assays, we confirmed that the interaction between phosphorylated Lrp1 and Shc1 also occurs in macrophages (Figure 13A).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 13A.

claim: The induction of Akt phosphorylation and Abca1 expression in response to oxLDL was significantly impaired by the knockdown of Shc1 in Ldlr−/− macrophages.
source: The induction of Akt phosphorylation and Abca1 expression in response to oxLDL was significantly impaired by the knockdown of Shc1 in Ldlr−/− macrophages, whereas Shc1 knock-down had no effect on Akt phosphorylation and Abca1 expression in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− macrophages (Figure 13B).
evidence: This claim is supported by shRNA knockdown data shown in Figure 13B.

claim: Shc1 knock-down had no effect on Akt phosphorylation and Abca1 expression in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− macrophages.
source: The induction of Akt phosphorylation and Abca1 expression in response to oxLDL was significantly impaired by the knockdown of Shc1 in Ldlr−/− macrophages, whereas Shc1 knock-down had no effect on Akt phosphorylation and Abca1 expression in Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− macrophages (Figure 13B).
evidence: This claim is supported by shRNA knockdown data shown in Figure 13B.

claim: Akt phosphorylation and Abca1 expression is dependent on the interaction between Shc1 and phosphorylated Lrp1.
source: We therefore concluded that Akt phosphorylation and Abca1 expression is dependent on the interaction between Shc1 and phosphorylated Lrp1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the shRNA knockdown data.

claim: Tyrosine phosphorylation of LRP1 is mediated by activated Src family tyrosine kinases in a range of inflammatory or proliferative conditions.
source: Collectively, our data provide a novel mechanistic basis for the role of macrophage LRP1 in atherogenesis. As summarized in Figure 14A, tyrosine phosphorylation of LRP1, which is mediated by activated Src family tyrosine kinases in a range of inflammatory or proliferative conditions (van der Geer, 2002), is required for interaction with the adaptor protein SHC1, which in turn augments PI3K/AKT activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to van der Geer, 2002.

claim: Tyrosine phosphorylation of LRP1 is required for interaction with the adaptor protein SHC1, which in turn augments PI3K/AKT activation.
source: Collectively, our data provide a novel mechanistic basis for the role of macrophage LRP1 in atherogenesis. As summarized in Figure 14A, tyrosine phosphorylation of LRP1, which is mediated by activated Src family tyrosine kinases in a range of inflammatory or proliferative conditions (van der Geer, 2002), is required for interaction with the adaptor protein SHC1, which in turn augments PI3K/AKT activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Phospho-AKT modulates PPARγ/LXR driven gene expression of which ABCA1 is a prominent target.
source: Phospho-AKT modulates PPARγ/LXR driven gene expression of which ABCA1 is a prominent target with well-documented roles in lipid metabolism and atherosclerosis (Aiello et al., 2002; Huang et al., 2015; Rader et al., 2009; Shao et al., 2014; Singaraja et al., 2002; Su et al., 2005; Tall and Yvan-Charvet, 2015; Yvan-Charvet et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The activation of the LRP1/SHC1/PI3K/AKT/PPARγ/LXR axis is necessary for the full effect of nuclear hormone receptor ligand-induced and PPARγ/LXR-dependent expression of ABCA1 and MerTK.
source: The activation of this LRP1/SHC1/PI3K/AKT/PPARγ/LXR axis is necessary for the full effect of nuclear hormone receptor ligand-induced and PPARγ/LXR-dependent expression of ABCA1 and the engulfment receptor MerTK.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: In the absence of LRP1/SHC1 interaction, the decreased expression of atheroprotective LXR target genes in macrophages leads to increased intracellular lipid accumulation, macrophage foam cell formation, impaired apoptotic cell clearance and increased atherosclerotic plaque formation.
source: In the absence of LRP1/SHC1 interaction, the decreased expression of atheroprotective LXR target genes in macrophages, as exemplified here by ABCA1 and MerTK, leads to increased intracellular lipid accumulation, macrophage foam cell formation, impaired apoptotic cell clearance and thus increased atherosclerotic plaque formation, independent of systemic lipid levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: LRP1 associates with lipid rafts in the plasma membrane, creating transient microdomains that are cell specific.
source: LRP1 associates with lipid rafts in the plasma membrane, thus creating transient microdomains that are cell specific (Wu and Gonias, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wu and Gonias, 2005.

claim: Through cellular cholesterol export ABCA1 regulates cellular plasma membrane cholesterol content and membrane structural organization, specifically the formation of lipid rafts.
source: Through cellular cholesterol export ABCA1 regulates cellular plasma membrane cholesterol content and membrane structural organization, specifically the formation of lipid rafts (Ito et al., 2015; Sezgin et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the setting of inflammation or cholesterol loading, increased proximity of LRP1 with activated Src family kinases in lipid rafts favors LRP1 tyrosine phosphorylation.
source: In the setting of inflammation or cholesterol loading, increased proximity of LRP1 with activated Src family kinases in lipid rafts favors LRP1 tyrosine phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data and established knowledge about lipid rafts.

claim: The induction of ABCA1 leads to reduction of lipid raft cholesterol content and dissociation of LRP1 from lipid rafts, creating a self-limiting negative feedback loop.
source: The induction of ABCA1 leads to reduction of lipid raft cholesterol content (Ito et al., 2015) and dissociation of LRP1 from lipid rafts, thus creating a self-limiting negative feedback loop and returning homeostatic balance to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data and a citation to Ito et al., 2015.

claim: By modulating membrane cholesterol content and lipid raft organization, macrophage ABCA1 regulates trafficking of Toll-like-receptor 4 (TLR4) to lipid rafts.
source: By modulating membrane cholesterol content and lipid raft organization, macrophage ABCA1 regulates trafficking of Toll-like-receptor 4 (TLR4) to lipid rafts (Zhu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhu et al., 2010.

claim: In lipid rafts, TLR4 forms a complex with TLR6 and oxLDL-binding CD36, which leads to recruitment of the adaptor MyD88, triggering inflammatory signaling.
source: In lipid rafts, TLR4 forms a complex with TLR6 and oxLDL-binding CD36 (Figure 14B and C), which leads to recruitment of the adaptor MyD88, thus triggering inflammatory signaling (Stewart et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stewart et al., 2010.

claim: ABCA1 has anti-inflammatory properties, as interaction of ApoA1 with ABCA1 activates JAK2/STAT3.
source: ABCA1 itself has anti-inflammatory properties, as interaction of ApoA1 with ABCA1 activates JAK2/STAT3 (Tang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tang et al., 2009.

claim: Induction of Abca1 by LXRs inhibits inflammatory NF-κB and MAPK signaling pathways downstream of TLRs.
source: Finally, as demonstrated by Ito et al, induction of Abca1 by LXRs inhibits inflammatory NF-κB and MAPK signaling pathways downstream of TLRs (Ito et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ito et al., 2015.

claim: By modulating LXR-driven ABCA1 gene expression through the SHC1/PI3K/AKT/PPARγ/LXRα axis, LRP1 is a pivotal regulator of the metabolic as well as inflammatory processes underlying atherosclerosis.
source: Therefore, by modulating LXR-driven ABCA1 gene expression through the SHC1/PI3K/AKT/PPARγ/LXRα axis, LRP1 is presenting itself as a pivotal regulator of the metabolic as well as inflammatory processes underlying atherosclerosis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data and discussion.

claim: LRP1 can directly regulate inflammatory gene transcription in macrophages.
source: In addition to the indirect anti-inflammatory effect through ABCA1, there is also emerging data that LRP1 can directly regulate inflammatory gene transcription in macrophages (Zurhove et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zurhove et al., 2008.

claim: After cleavage of the LRP1 intracellular domain (ICD) by γ-secretase from the plasma membrane, the LRP1 ICD translocates into the nucleus and acts as a transcriptional repressor of genes for inflammatory cytokines.
source: After cleavage of the LRP1 intracellular domain (ICD) by γ-secretase from the plasma membrane, the LRP1 ICD translocates into the nucleus and acts as a transcriptional repressor of genes for inflammatory cytokines (Figure 14B) (Zurhove et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zurhove et al., 2008.

claim: In endothelial cells, the LRP1 ICD has been shown to directly interact with PPARγ and function as a transcriptional co-regulator of the PPARγ target gene Pdk4.
source: In an analogous manner in endothelial cells, the LRP1 ICD has been shown to directly interact with PPARγ and function as a transcriptional co-regulator of the PPARγ target gene Pdk4 (Mao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mao et al., 2017.

claim: Macrophage-specific deficiency of LRP1 is associated with increased macrophage apoptosis and decreased efferocytosis, leading to larger necrotic cores in atherosclerotic plaque.
source: Macrophage-specific deficiency of LRP1 is associated with increased macrophage apoptosis and decreased efferocytosis, leading to larger necrotic cores in atherosclerotic plaque (Misra and Pizzo, 2005; Yancey et al., 2010; Yancey et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Macrophage-specific deficiency of LRP1 has been associated with reduced levels of pAKT.
source: Mechanistically, this has been associated with reduced levels of pAKT (Yancey et al., 2010), similar to the findings in our Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yancey et al., 2010.

claim: LXR-deficient macrophages have reduced phagocytic capacity, which is associated with decreased expression of Mertk.
source: LXR-deficient macrophages have reduced phagocytic capacity (A-Gonzalez et al., 2009), which is associated with decreased expression of Mertk, an LXR-responsive gene.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to A-Gonzalez et al., 2009.

claim: MerTK is critical for efficient macrophage phagocytosis and efferocytosis, and deficiencies in macrophage MerTK expression contribute to increased necrotic cores in atherosclerotic lesions.
source: MerTK is critical for efficient macrophage phagocytosis and efferocytosis, and deficiencies in macrophage MerTK expression contribute to increased necrotic cores in atherosclerotic lesions (Li et al., 2006; Scott et al., 2001; Thorp et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LRP1 is necessary for the efficient phagocytosis of apoptotic cells, as it is required for the formation of a multiprotein complex involving LRP1, the receptor tyrosine kinase AXL, and the scaffolding protein RANBP9.
source: Finally, LRP1 itself is necessary for the efficient phagocytosis of apoptotic cells, as it is required for the formation of a multiprotein complex involving LRP1, the receptor tyrosine kinase AXL, and the scaffolding protein RANBP9 (Subramanian et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Subramanian et al., 2014.

claim: AXL is involved in the recognition and binding of apoptotic cells, while LRP1, by associating with GULP1, is required for the final engulfment of the dead cells.
source: As described by Subramanian et al., whereas AXL is involved in the recognition and binding of apoptotic cells, LRP1, by associating with GULP1 (Su et al., 2002), is required for the final engulfment of the dead cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Subramanian et al. and Su et al., 2002.

claim: The results showing an identical atherogenic lipoprotein profile upon cholesterol-feeding of Ldlr−/− mice transplanted with Ldlr−/− or Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− bone marrow differ from those of Bi et al., who showed reduced plasma lipid levels in mice lacking Abca1 completely in their monocytes/macrophages.
source: Our results, which show an identical atherogenic lipoprotein profile upon cholesterol-feeding of Ldlr−/− mice transplanted with Ldlr−/− or Lrp1Y63F;Ldlr−/− bone marrow, differ on first glance from those of Bi et al. (Bi et al., 2014), who showed reduced plasma lipid levels in mice lacking Abca1 completely in their monocytes/macrophages.
evidence: This claim compares the current results to a previous study by Bi et al., 2014.

claim: In the Bi et al. model, elevated plasma cholesterol levels induced by cholesterol feeding led to cholesterol overload of circulating cells, which secreted inflammatory cytokines that reduced VLDL secretion by the liver, resulting in a less atherogenic plasma lipid profile.
source: In their model, however, elevated plasma cholesterol levels induced by cholesterol feeding and the resulting cholesterol overload of circulating cells led to the secretion of inflammatory cytokines, which reduced VLDL secretion by the liver and thus resulted in a less atherogenic plasma lipid profile, which subsided on a low cholesterol chow diet.
evidence: This claim describes the mechanism in the Bi et al. study.

claim: Monocyte/macrophages carrying the Y63F mutation in Lrp1 retain residual, though substantially lower, Abca1 expression, which would protect the circulating cells from cholesterol overload in a hyperlipidemic, cholesterol-fed state.
source: In our case, monocyte/macrophages carrying the Y63F mutation in Lrp1 retain residual, though substantially lower, Abca1 expression, which would protect the circulating cells from cholesterol overload in a hyperlipidemic, cholesterol-fed state.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data showing residual Abca1 expression.

claim: The current studies have revealed a novel mechanism through which macrophage LRP1 not only regulates ABCA1 expression to maintain cholesterol efflux, but also integrates cellular cholesterol homeostasis with inflammation and efferocytosis.
source: In conclusion, our current studies have revealed a novel mechanism through which macrophage LRP1 not only regulates ABCA1 expression to maintain cholesterol efflux, but also integrates cellular cholesterol homeostasis with inflammation and efferocytosis.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: These macrophage-specific processes demonstrate the atheroprotective role of LRP1 in mechanisms distinct from those found in SMCs.
source: In aggregate, these macrophage-specific processes demonstrate the atheroprotective role of LRP1 in mechanisms distinct from those found in SMCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing different effects in macrophages versus SMCs.

claim: These results underscore the cell-specific nature of LRP1-mediated signaling and highlight the central role of LRP1 in integrating cellular cholesterol homeostasis with other atheroprotective processes.
source: Together, these results underscore the cell-specific nature of LRP1-mediated signaling and highlight the central role of LRP1 in integrating cellular cholesterol homeostasis with other atheroprotective processes.
evidence: This claim summarizes the broader implications of the study.
